name: Inverted
description:
An Inverted Hover maintains the helicopter upside-down in a stationary position through continuous negative collective input. All lift logic is reversed: negative collective now pushes the craft upward (from your perspective), and cyclic axis mapping requires careful re-learning before committing any real airspace.

### Execution Steps
1. From a stable upright hover at a safe altitude (minimum 10-12 feet), smoothly roll inverted using aileron.
2. The instant you pass 90 degrees of roll, apply negative collective to arrest altitude loss. The helicopter should settle into an inverted stationary position.
3. Cyclic pitch is now reversed relative to the ground: pushing forward (stick up) moves the inverted nose upward in the air. Aileron remains the same direction visually but acts against gravity from the opposite side. Confirm the axis mapping in your head before attempting.
4. Use rudder to keep the inverted nose pointed away from you (tail-in orientation still applies in the inverted state).
5. To exit, roll back upright using aileron and immediately transition to positive collective to catch the altitude drop.

### Common Problems
- **Negative Collective Delay:** Hesitating even briefly after passing 90 degrees of roll causes rapid altitude loss. Commit to negative pitch the instant you cross inverted — there is no grace period.
- **Orientation Blur:** The canopy now points at the ground. Many pilots exit inverted tail-in into an unintended nose-in upright hover. Know your exit heading explicitly before going inverted.
- **Tail Rotor Compensation Shift:** Tail rotor thrust reverses effectiveness when inverted. You will likely need opposite rudder trim to hold the same heading compared to your upright hover settings.
